newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Price, wage pact seen key to Hungary inflation drop.
newsitem.headline: Price, wage pact seen key to Hungary inflation drop.

text.p: Hungary could push inflation below 10 percent in 1998 if the government reaches a satisfactory prices and wages agreement with employers and unions, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Tuesday.
"From a pure economic sense, this is possible," Deputy Secretary of State Tamas Tetenyi told Reuters.
But Tetenyi said such conditions depended on a determination from all sections of society to resist inflationary pressures.

Economic figures in the past few years had sparked higher inflation expectations than government forecasts, which resulted in larger wage claims and price rises than necessary, Tetenyi said. This was an important factor which itself could limit the pace of reduction in inflation, he said.
"While these social behaviour patterns exist, a dramatic fall in inflation, for example from 18 percent to eight percent, cannot happen," he said.
"The condition (of single-digit inflation in 1998) comes from a social-political will (to keep inflation down), which should appear in all price and wage bargaining," Tetenyi added.
Tetenyi declined to predict the chances of such a wide social consensus on wages and prices before the 1998 elections, which are expected to add upward pressure on wages and prices.
According to government plans, Hungary should reduce 1997 inflation to between 16 and 18 percent from 23.6 percent in 1996. In 1998, inflation is expected to drop another five percentage points.

But Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told the daily Magyar Hirlap on Monday that Hungary, urged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cut inflation more quickly, may revise its 1998 economic policy plans to include a larger inflation cut than previously planned.
Tetenyi said economic factors do not justify inflation remaining as high as 13 percent in 1998. Instead, he said inflation could drop to between eight and nine percent next year.
A monthly Reuters poll in January showed that analysts expected inflation to drop to around 18.5 percent in 1997 and 15.75 percent in 1998.
